どこ です か — Where is it?
You ask where something is, say what there is in a place (あります / います) and where things are: on, under, next to, in.
There’s a book on the desk.
There’s a cat under the chair.
The bank is next to the station.
To use ここ / そこ / あそこ / どこ (here / there / over there / where).
To tell あります (things) from います (people and animals).
To say what there is somewhere: X に Y が あります.
To say position: つくえ の うえ / いす の した / えき の となり.
To ask the way to the toilet, the station, the bank.
Mihai wants to borrow a Japanese book from the university library in Madrid. He bumps into Yuki.
Oh, Mihai! The library is over there. It’s that white building.
Yuki! Hello. Are there Japanese books in the library?
They’re on the second floor. The lift is there.
The toilet is next to the lift.
(On the second floor) Look, here are the Japanese books.
Ah! There’s a cat under the desk!
Hee-hee. That cat is the library cat. Her name is Tama.
There’s a cat in the library? Amazing!
Tama is here every day. She loves books.
エレベーター has two long vowels: e-re-BEH-TAH. Hold each “ー” for an extra beat.
こう = “koh”, a long vowel: gin-koh. If you shorten it, nobody will understand you!
As with です, the final u in います and あります is barely heard: “imas”, “arimas”.
In chapter 2 you learned これ / それ / あれ (this / that). The same KO-SO-A-DO system works for PLACES too:
The most useful travel sentence in Japanese: “X は どこ です か” (Where is X?). It works for anything: えき, トイレ, ぎんこう, ホテル.
2. あります or います? Living or non-living
Japanese has two verbs for “to exist / to be somewhere”. The choice depends on whether the thing is ALIVE (moves by itself) or not:
ほん, つくえ, えき, き (tree)
The classic mistake: “ねこ が あります”. A cat is alive → います. Japanese people will understand, but it will sound as if the cat were a toy!
Negative: ありません / いません. E.g.: トイレ が ありません (There’s no toilet).
3. “What’s there?”: X に Y が あります
To say what is in a place, the structure is: PLACE に THING が あります / います. The particle に marks the PLACE, and が marks the new thing you’re learning about.
There’s a cat in the library.
There’s a desk in the room.
It’s just like Spanish! “En la biblioteca HAY un gato” = としょかん に ねこ が います. And the verb comes at the end, as usual.
4. “Where is that thing?”: Y は X に あります
When the thing is already known and you’re asking WHERE it is, you put it first, with は:
PLACE に THING が あります
にかい に ほん が あります。 (There are books on the second floor.)
THING は PLACE に あります
ほん は にかい に あります。 (The books are on the second floor.)
Again like Spanish: HAY (something new) versus ESTÁ (something known). は ≈ “está”, が ≈ “hay”. In English: “there is” versus “it is”.
Even simpler: “ほん は にかい です” (The books are on the second floor). です can replace に あります.
5. Positions: うえ, した, なか, となり…
Positions are nouns. You link them with の: “the desk’s top” = つくえ の うえ (on the desk).
There’s a laptop on the desk.
The order is the reverse of English: English “UNDER the chair”, Japanese “chair-の UNDER” (いす の した).
The cat is alive → います.
The book isn’t alive → あります.
There’s a cat under the desk.
ゆきさん の へや — Yuki’s room
Yuki describes her room in Madrid in a message to her mother in Tokyo.
In the room there’s a desk, a chair and a bed.
On the desk there’s a laptop and some Spanish books.
Next to the bed there’s a window. In front of the window there’s a tree.
In the tree there’s a bird. It sings every morning.
Near the house there’s a convenience store and a bank. The station is close too.
But it’s different from the shops in Japan. They don’t have onigiri!
What don’t the shops in Madrid have?
えき は とおい です か。 (Is the station far?)
タマ は どこ です か — Where’s Tama?
It’s morning. This is the university library.
There are lots of books in the library. There are lots of people too.
And there’s also a cat. Her name is Tama.
Every day Tama is under the desk.
But today she isn’t there. Yuki is worried.
“Mihai, Tama isn’t here! Where is Tama?”
Mihai and Yuki look for Tama.
She isn’t on the chair. She isn’t behind the bookshelf either.
She isn’t in front of the toilet or in the lift.
On the ground floor there’s the reception. At reception there’s an old lady.
“Tama? She’s over there, you know. Next to the window.”
Next to the window there’s a small box.
Tama is in the box. And… there are three kittens!
Now there are four cats in the library.
Yuki goes there every day. But she doesn’t read many books.
いま、ねこ は なんびき います か。 (How many cats are there now?)
あります / います and the particles
There’s a book in the bag.
Kenji explains to Mihai how to find his way around Osaka station.
There are lots of shops and restaurants in the station.
The toilet is next to the ticket gates.
There are lots of taxis in front of the station.
Where’s the map? It’s over there.
What’s in front of the station?
Interesting: for the taxis, Kenji uses います. Why do you think that is?
Because they have a driver (a person) and they move
Because there are lots of them
Japanese people sometimes use います for vehicles with a driver, as if they were “alive”.
